title: The Game Loop
summary: Every real-time game is built around one loop that runs as long as the game does: read **input**, **update** the world, **render** a frame, repeat, dozens of times a second. This lesson builds that loop step by step, explains what belongs in each phase, and shows how an engine is organised around it.
markdown:
## The heart of every game A word processor waits for the user to do something. A game does not wait: monsters move, timers tick and the screen redraws whether or not the player touches anything. So at the centre of every game engine is a loop: ```mermaid flowchart LR I["Process input
keys, mouse, pad, network"] --> U["Update
move, collide, think, animate"] U --> R["Render
draw the current state"] R --> I ``` Each trip round the loop produces one **frame**. At 60 frames per second the whole loop has 16.7 ms (lesson 8.08). ```cpp #include #include struct World { float x{ 0 }; float speed{ 2.0f }; int frames{ 0 }; bool running{ true }; }; void processInput(World&) { /* read keys; set flags such as world.running = false on Escape */ } void update(World& w, float dt) { w.x += w.speed * dt; // move 2 units per second, however long the frame was ++w.frames; if (w.x >= 1.0f) w.running = false; } void render(const World& w) { std::cout << "frame " << w.frames << ": x = " << w.x << '\n'; } int main() { World world; const float dt{ 0.1f }; // pretend each frame takes 0.1 s, so the output is the same every run while (world.running) { processInput(world); update(world, dt); render(world); } return 0; } ``` ``` frame 1: x = 0.2 frame 2: x = 0.4 frame 3: x = 0.6 frame 4: x = 0.8 frame 5: x = 1 ``` A real game measures `dt` with a clock (lesson 5.07) instead of pretending; the next lesson covers how to use it well. ## What goes in each phase | Phase | Does | Must not | |---|---|---| | **Input** | Drain the window messages (lesson 5.05's `PeekMessage` loop), read devices, turn them into actions (lesson 10.05) | Change the world directly | | **Update** | Advance the simulation by `dt`: movement, physics, AI, timers, animation, game rules, spawning and removing entities | Draw anything, or wait for anything | | **Render** | Draw the world **as it is now**: sprites, models, effects, interface | Change the world | Keeping these separate is what lets engines run update at a fixed rate while rendering as fast as possible (lesson 10.02), run rendering on another thread, record and replay input, or run a server with no rendering at all. ## The engine around the loop An engine is mostly the systems that the loop calls each frame: ```mermaid flowchart TB L["Game loop"] --> IN["Input system"] L --> SIM["Simulation
entities and components (10.03)"] SIM --> PH["Physics and collision"] SIM --> AI["AI and scripts (10.08)"] SIM --> AN["Animation"] L --> AU["Audio"] L --> RE["Renderer (10.04)"] RES["Resource manager (10.06)"] --> RE RES --> AU RES --> SIM ``` A small game calls these in a fixed order on one thread. A large engine spreads their work across worker threads with a job system (lesson 6.05) while keeping the same overall order, because order matters: physics must run after movement is decided and before rendering, or the frame shows stale positions. ## Starting and stopping Around the loop sit **initialisation** (create the window, load the first level, start subsystems in dependency order) and **shutdown** (stop them in the reverse order, as RAII does for objects, lesson 2.04). Many engine bugs are ordering bugs here: audio shut down before the entities that still play sounds, a resource released before the renderer stops using it. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Updating in the render phase > Rendering must only read the state, or the result depends on how often frames are drawn. > [!warning] Waiting inside the loop > Blocking on a file, the network or a lock stalls every frame. Move slow work to other threads (lesson 6.05) and check its result each frame. > [!warning] Moving by a fixed amount per frame > `x += 2` moves twice as fast at 120 fps as at 60. Multiply by `dt`. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is a frame? + One pass of the loop: input, one update, one image - One sixtieth of a second, whatever the game is doing - One image stored in the GPU's memory - One call to the operating system's message loop > Frames are not tied to a fixed length of time; how long one takes depends on the work in it. ? Why keep input, update and render separate? + So each can run at its own rate, and rendering never changes the world - Because the compiler requires them to be in separate functions - Because rendering must happen before input each frame - So that each phase can use a different programming language > If rendering changed game state, the game would behave differently depending on the frame rate. Separating them also lets input be recorded and replayed. ? Why does the order of systems in the update matter? - Because systems that run later get more time - Because the order decides which systems are drawn on top + Later systems use earlier ones' results, or see stale data - It does not; systems are independent by design > Running collision before movement, for example, checks positions from the previous frame. ? What are the three phases of the game loop? + Input, update, render - Load, play, then save - Compile, link, then run > They repeat every frame for as long as the game runs. ? Why should rendering never change the game state? - Rendering is too slow + The state would depend on how many frames get drawn - The GPU cannot write to memory > Updates belong in the update phase, driven by time. ? Why multiply speeds by `dt`? - To make the game run faster - Because the compiler requires it + So movement per second is the same at any frame rate > A fixed step per frame makes speed depend on frame rate. ```
ideas:
- Change `dt` in the example to 0.05 and predict how many frames it takes to reach x = 1.
- Combine this loop with lesson 5.06's window, measuring real `dt` with `QueryPerformanceCounter`.
- List, for a game you like, which systems would run in the update phase each frame.
